headline: Sand to Silicon: Chip Manufacturing Deep Dive
summary: From beach sand to 3nm transistors — the incredible journey powering every AI model and smartphone. Understanding this supply chain reveals why compute costs what it does and where bottlenecks lie.
source: General Semiconductor Industry Knowledge & Manufacturing Processes

slides.title: Your Phone Started as Beach Sand
slides.subtitle: The hidden supply chain turning quartz into trillion-transistor chips
slides.body: Every AI model, smartphone, and GPU traces back to ultra-pure silicon refined from common sand. The journey spans continents, extreme physics, and the most complex manufacturing process humans have ever built.
slides.deep_dive: Silicon makes up 28% of Earth's crust, but semiconductor-grade silicon requires 99.9999999% purity — 'nine nines.' This means one impurity atom per billion silicon atoms. Achieving this starts with metallurgical-grade silicon from quartzite smelted in electric arc furnaces, then refined via the Siemens process using trichlorosilane gas decomposition. The resulting polysilicon rods are melted and pulled into single-crystal ingots using the Czochralski method, where a seed crystal rotates and slowly withdraws from molten silicon, forming a perfect cylindrical boule up to 300mm in diameter. This crystal structure is critical — any dislocation or defect propagates through billions of transistors.
slides.key_fact: Semiconductor silicon is 1 billion times purer than beach sand.
slides.why_it_matters: Compute scarcity starts at the atomic level — purity limits yield, yield limits supply, supply limits AI training capacity.

slides.title: AI Demand Exploded the Fab Queue
slides.subtitle: Training clusters consume wafer starts faster than new fabs come online
slides.body: LLM training clusters now demand thousands of cutting-edge GPUs each. A single H100 wafer yields ~90 dies; a 100k-GPU cluster needs ~1,100 wafers — months of dedicated 4nm/3nm capacity. Foundries are sold out through 2026.
slides.deep_dive: The semiconductor industry operates on a 3-5 year fab construction cycle. TSMC's Arizona fab broke ground in 2021; volume production starts 2025. Meanwhile, NVIDIA's data center revenue grew from $15B (FY2023) to $47.5B (FY2024) — a 3x surge in 12 months. This demand shock hit when EUV lithography (essential for 7nm and below) was only available from one supplier: ASML. Each EUV scanner costs ~$150M and takes 18 months to build. The result: a structural supply constraint where leading-edge capacity allocation became a geopolitical lever. Governments now subsidize domestic fabs (CHIPS Act, EU Chips Act) not just for economics, but for sovereign AI compute.
slides.key_fact: Leading-edge fab capacity is allocated years in advance — new customers wait 24+ months.
slides.why_it_matters: Your cloud GPU quota and API rate limits trace back to wafer allocation decisions made in 2022.

slides.title: Photolithography: Printing Atoms with Light
slides.subtitle: EUV light at 13.5nm wavelength writes 3nm features through quantum tricks
slides.body: Modern chips use extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography — light so short it's absorbed by air, requiring vacuum chambers and mirrors smoother than 0.3nm roughness.
slides.deep_dive: Photolithography is the heart of chipmaking: coat wafer with photoresist → expose pattern via mask → develop (wash away exposed/unexposed areas) → etch (transfer pattern into underlying layer) → strip resist → repeat. At 3nm, features are smaller than the 193nm wavelength of deep UV light. The solution: EUV at 13.5nm, generated by vaporizing tin droplets with a CO2 laser 50,000 times per second. The 'mirrors' are actually multilayer Bragg reflectors — 40-50 alternating layers of molybdenum and silicon, each ~7nm thick, reflecting EUV via constructive interference. Even then, resolution requires computational lithography: the mask pattern bears little resemblance to the final feature, pre-distorted by inverse algorithms so diffraction produces the target shape. Multiple patterning (SAQP, LELE) stitches exposures together for features below single-exposure limits.
slides.key_fact: EUV mirrors are the smoothest human-made objects — if scaled to Earth size, tallest bump would be 1cm.
slides.why_it_matters: EUV access determines who makes leading-edge chips. Only TSMC, Samsung, and Intel have high-volume EUV lines.

steps.title: Coat
steps.desc: Spin photoresist onto wafer — uniform layer ~50-100nm thick

steps.title: Expose
steps.desc: EUV scanner projects mask pattern through vacuum onto resist

steps.title: Develop
steps.desc: Chemical wash removes soluble resist regions, leaving pattern

steps.title: Etch
steps.desc: Plasma transfers pattern into silicon, oxide, or metal layers

steps.title: Strip & Repeat
steps.desc: Remove resist, inspect, repeat for 80-100+ layers per chip

slides.title: Incumbents vs. The Rest of the World
slides.subtitle: Three companies control leading-edge logic; everyone else designs or assembles
slides.body: TSMC, Samsung, Intel manufacture at 3nm/5nm. Design houses (NVIDIA, AMD, Apple) rent capacity. Assembly/test (ASE, Amkor) and equipment (ASML, Applied Materials) form the moat.
slides.deep_dive: The semiconductor value chain has split into specialized layers: Foundries (TSMC 60%+ foundry share) invest $30-40B/year in capex to push process nodes. Fabless designers (NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Apple) focus on architecture, paying per-wafer. EDA tools (Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens) enable design at scale — a single 3nm tapeout costs $500M+. Equipment makers (ASML monopoly on EUV, Applied Materials/Lam Research/KLA for deposition/etch/metrology) capture value via IP. Assembly & test (OSATs) handle packaging — now critical as 3D stacking (TSMC CoWoS, Intel Foveros) becomes the performance driver post-Moore's Law. Geopolitics fractures this: US export controls block EUV and advanced node access to China; Taiwan concentration risk drives 'friend-shoring' to Arizona, Japan, Germany.
slides.key_fact: TSMC alone produces ~90% of world's advanced logic chips (<7nm).
slides.why_it_matters: Your chip vendor's roadmap depends on TSMC's capacity allocation — not their engineering talent.
right_items: OSAT: ASE, Amkor — advanced packaging bottleneck
Materials: Merck, JSR — photoresist IP moats

slides.title: Your Model Size Is a Supply Chain Decision
slides.subtitle: Parameter count maps directly to wafer starts and HBM capacity
slides.body: A 70B parameter model needs ~140GB VRAM (BF16) — 8x H100 80GB. That's 8 GPUs, ~0.09 wafers at 4nm. A 1T parameter model needs ~112 GPUs — 1.2 wafers. Wafer allocation dictates what's trainable.
slides.deep_dive: The semiconductor supply chain imposes hard constraints on AI engineering: 1) GPU availability — H100 lead times 52+ weeks in 2023-24, now easing but B200/GB200 ramping. 2) Memory bandwidth — HBM3E stacks (12-hi, 36GB) require advanced packaging (CoWoS-L) capacity, a separate bottleneck from logic wafers. 3) Interconnect — NVLink/NVLink Switch scaling laws mean cluster size hits packaging limits before network limits. 4) Power/cooling — 100k GPU clusters need 100MW+; data center build-out is 2-3 years. Smart engineers optimize for compute efficiency (Mixture of Experts, quantization, distillation) not just model quality. The best architecture is the one you can actually deploy on allocated silicon.
slides.key_fact: HBM packaging capacity (CoWoS) is now tighter than logic wafer capacity for AI chips.
slides.why_it_matters: Model architecture choices are implicitly fab capacity requests. Design for the silicon you'll get, not the silicon you want.

slides.title: Compute Is the New Oil — And It's Mined from Sand
slides.subtitle: The entire AI revolution rests on a supply chain with 3 choke points
slides.body: Three bottlenecks control global AI capacity: EUV scanners (ASML), leading-edge wafers (TSMC), advanced packaging (CoWoS). Every model, API, and startup competes for slices of this fixed pie.
slides.deep_dive: The semiconductor industry has become the limiting reagent of artificial intelligence. Unlike software, where marginal cost is near zero, compute has physics-enforced scarcity: atomic purity requirements, quantum-limited lithography, thermal limits on 3D stacking, and multi-year fab cycles. This creates a new strategic landscape: nations subsidize fabs for sovereignty; hyperscalers design custom silicon (TPU, Trainium, Maia) to reduce TSMC dependence; startups optimize for inference efficiency over training scale. The winners in the next decade will be those who treat compute as a constrained resource — architecting models, systems, and products that maximize intelligence per wafer. The sand-to-silicon journey isn't trivia — it's the balance sheet of the AI economy.
slides.key_fact: Every AI breakthrough is ultimately a materials science and logistics victory.
slides.why_it_matters: Strategic advantage shifts from 'who has the best model' to 'who secures the compute to run it.'
takeaways: Treat GPU quota as a capital allocation problem — optimize intelligence per watt per wafer
Diversify inference targets (CPU, edge NPU, custom ASIC) to reduce single-fab dependency
Track packaging capacity (CoWoS, SoIC) — it's the new bottleneck for memory-bound workloads

_story.title: Sand to Silicon: Your Phone's Secret Origin
_story.hook: Did You Know your powerful smartphone began as humble beach sand? 🤯
_story.headline: From Grains of Sand to the Brains of Your Devices
_story.fact_summary: The incredible microchips that power your smartphone, computer, and smart devices actually begin as one of Earth's most common materials: sand. Through an elaborate and precise manufacturing process, ordinary silicon dioxide from sand is purified into ultra-pure silicon crystals, then meticulously carved and layered to create billions of microscopic transistors. It's like transforming beach grains into the intricate, intelligent 'brains' of our entire digital world!
_story.source: General Semiconductor Industry Knowledge & Manufacturing Processes
